config.title: Portal Navigation

intro.title: Portal Navigation
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a multi-page portal application with navigation between different sections like Dashboard, Profile, and Settings. You'll learn how to implement client-side routing using Angular's Router module to create seamless navigation without full page reloads. The core concept focuses on defining routes, configuring the router, and using router outlets to dynamically display different components based on the current URL. You'll work with key Angular constructs including RouterModule, Route configuration, router-outlet directive, and routerLink directive to create clickable navigation links. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to structure a navigable Angular application and provide users with intuitive ways to move between different views.
intro.usecase: Portal navigation patterns are essential in enterprise applications like admin dashboards, content management systems, and multi-tenant SaaS platforms where users need to switch between different organizational contexts or workspaces. You'll find this pattern in products like GitHub's organization switcher, Slack's workspace navigation, or Azure's subscription/resource group selectors. As a developer, you'll implement portal navigation when building applications that serve multiple clients, departments, or projects, allowing users to seamlessly switch contexts while maintaining their session state. This pattern is particularly common in B2B applications where users belong to multiple organizations or need to manage different data scopes within the same application interface.

objectives: Implement Angular router configuration for multiple navigation routes
Construct a navigation menu component with routing links
Configure route parameters to pass data between portal sections
Apply router guards to control access to protected portal areas
Integrate active route highlighting to indicate current navigation state
Manipulate browser navigation using programmatic routing methods
Bind click events to trigger navigation between portal components

steps.title: Initialize Navigation Items
steps.instruction: Inside the PortalComponent class, create a property called navigationItems that contains an array of navigation objects, each with a title and route property
steps.hint: Define a class property as an array containing objects with title and route properties. This will serve as the data source for your navigation menu.
steps.expectedOutcome: The PortalComponent will have a navigationItems property containing an array of navigation menu items with titles and routes
successCriteria: navigationItems property is defined as an array containing objects with title and route properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your navigationItems property contains an array of objects with both title and route properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigationItems property should be an array of objects, where each object has a title and route property.

steps.title: Define Navigation Handler
steps.instruction: Create a navigateTo method inside the PortalComponent class that accepts a route parameter and uses the router.navigate method to programmatically navigate to that route.
steps.hint: Define a method that takes a route string as a parameter and calls this.router.navigate() with an array containing the route.
steps.expectedOutcome: The PortalComponent will have a navigateTo method that can programmatically navigate to different routes using the Angular Router.
successCriteria: The navigateTo method is defined, accepts a route parameter, and uses this.router.navigate() to change routes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your navigateTo method accepts a route parameter and uses this.router.navigate() to handle the navigation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigateTo method needs to accept a route parameter and use this.router.navigate() with an array containing the route to navigate programmatically.

steps.instruction: Add a @Component decorator with a template property that contains a div with class 'portal-container', an h1 element with text 'Portal Navigation', and a nav element with class 'navigation'.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator above your class with a template property containing the HTML structure. The template should have a container div, header, and navigation section.
steps.expectedOutcome: The PortalComponent will have a @Component decorator with a template containing the basic HTML structure for the portal interface with a container, header, and navigation section.
successCriteria: @Component decorator is added with a template property containing a div with class 'portal-container', an h1 element with 'Portal Navigation' text, and a nav element with class 'navigation'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your template includes all three elements: the container div with class 'portal-container', the h1 with 'Portal Navigation' text, and the nav element with class 'navigation'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template structure isn't complete. Add a @Component decorator with a template property containing a div (class 'portal-container'), h1 ('Portal Navigation'), and nav (class 'navigation') elements.

steps.hint: Use the *ngFor directive on an li element to iterate through the navigationItems array. Access the label property of each navigation item.

  • {{ item.name }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The portal will display a navigation menu as an unordered list with each navigation item's label rendered in a list item.
successCriteria: An unordered list is added with *ngFor directive that loops through navigationItems and displays each item's label in a list item.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Add Navigation Buttons
steps.instruction: Inside each list item, add a button element that displays the navigation item's title and calls the navigateTo method with the item's route when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the button element with Angular's (click) event binding to call navigateTo, and display the item.title inside the button text.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each navigation item will have a clickable button that shows the item title and triggers navigation when clicked.
successCriteria: Button elements are added inside each list item with (click) event binding to navigateTo method and display item.title text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure each button has both the (click) event binding to call navigateTo and displays the item.title text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons need to be inside the list items with (click) event binding to call navigateTo(item.route) and display {{item.title}} text.

steps.title: Wire Click Events to Navigation
steps.instruction: Add a (click) event binding to the button element that calls the navigateTo method with item.route as the argument.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (click)="methodName(parameter)" on the button element.
steps.expectedOutcome: Button elements will have click event handlers that call the navigateTo method with the appropriate route parameter.
successCriteria: Button has (click) event binding that calls navigateTo with item.route parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure the click handler calls navigateTo and passes item.route as the parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button needs a (click) event binding that calls navigateTo(item.route). Check your event binding syntax.
